research_problem: How should Riverton establish a wastewater surveillance program for respiratory and enteric infections, and how should its data be governed and communicated so that it supports public-health action without misleading or stigmatizing neighborhoods?
project_context: Riverton Public Health Department is partnering with Riverton University and the municipal Water Services Department to design a pilot wastewater-monitoring program for a city of roughly 280,000 residents. The team has completed an initial plan centered on citywide early warning and public reporting, but is revisiting that plan after receiving new operational and community information.
plan_document:
Riverton Wastewater Surveillance Planning Team — Existing Research Plan

Aim: Design a six-month pilot that determines whether wastewater measurements can provide useful early warning of selected infectious diseases in Riverton and establishes a credible approach for sharing the resulting information.

1. Research question 1: Can weekly wastewater measurements at Riverton's two treatment plants detect changes in SARS-CoV-2, influenza A, and norovirus before corresponding changes appear in citywide clinical reporting?

2. Research question 2: Which normalization and laboratory procedures produce sufficiently stable, interpretable trends across the two treatment-plant catchments, given variation in flow, rainfall, and population served?

3. Research question 3: What public-facing reporting format allows residents and decision-makers to understand citywide wastewater trends and their uncertainty, while maintaining trust in the program?

The pilot will compare wastewater signals with aggregated citywide emergency-department and laboratory reports, not individual-level records. The initial geographic unit is the two treatment-plant catchments: North Plant and South Plant. Results will be treated as trend indicators rather than estimates of disease prevalence.

Tasks
1. Dr. Maya Chen (epidemiology) will define lead-time metrics, obtain weekly aggregated clinical comparison data, and specify interpretation thresholds for SARS-CoV-2, influenza A, and norovirus.
2. Luis Ortega (environmental engineering) will document the North and South catchments, select influent sampling points at both plants, assess flow and rainfall effects, and develop a 24-hour composite-sampling protocol.
3. Priya Nair (environmental engineering) will validate RT-qPCR assays and compare normalization using pepper mild mottle virus and measured flow.
4. Dr. Hannah Brooks (science and technology studies) will interview public-health staff, water-utility staff, and residents about confidence in citywide reporting, then draft a public dashboard and uncertainty language.
5. Chen and Brooks will develop an escalation protocol linking sustained wastewater increases to internal public-health review and a public advisory when warranted.
6. Ortega will prepare a sampling, laboratory, and data-transfer budget for the six-month pilot.

old_questions: Can weekly measurements at the North and South treatment plants detect changes in SARS-CoV-2, influenza A, and norovirus before citywide clinical reporting?
Which normalization and laboratory procedures yield stable, interpretable trends across the two treatment-plant catchments?
What public-facing reporting format can communicate citywide wastewater trends and uncertainty while maintaining trust?
new_questions: Can twice-weekly measurements at three defined trunk-sewer subcatchments produce technically interpretable signals for SARS-CoV-2 and influenza A under local flow and rainfall conditions?

How can subcatchment wastewater signals and aggregated citywide clinical data be used together for internal public-health situational awareness, without assuming that wastewater will consistently lead clinical reporting?

What governance process, community participation, and interpretation criteria are required before any localized wastewater findings could be released, and what citywide descriptive communication is appropriate during the pilot?
what_changed_and_why: The geographic and technical focus moves from two heterogeneous treatment-plant catchments to three stable trunk-sewer subcatchments because North Plant stormwater intrusion and broad mixed catchments make plant-level trends difficult to interpret. (Direction Review — March 18, 2027)
The pathogen scope drops norovirus because its recovery is too variable for reliable pilot interpretation; the pilot retains SARS-CoV-2 and influenza A. (Direction Review — March 18, 2027)

The aim changes from demonstrating citywide lead time and building a public dashboard to assessing internally useful localized signals with clinical data as contextual validation, because lead time cannot be promised under the revised design. (Direction Review — March 18, 2027)

Public disclosure is deferred and localized public reporting is prohibited during the pilot because community partners warned that neighborhood-level displays could stigmatize communities and be overinterpreted. (Direction Review — March 18, 2027)
tasks_to_update: Update Chen's task from defining lead-time metrics for three pathogens to defining internal situational-awareness and interpretation criteria for SARS-CoV-2 and influenza A, while retaining acquisition of aggregated citywide clinical data as contextual validation. (Direction Review — March 18, 2027)

Replace Ortega's two-treatment-plant sampling and 24-hour composite protocol with documentation of three trunk-sewer subcatchments and a twice-weekly time-weighted composite protocol; revise the associated operational budget. (Direction Review — March 18, 2027)
Revise Nair's validation task to focus on SARS-CoV-2 and influenza A at the new sampling sites, and remove norovirus from routine pilot validation. (Direction Review — March 18, 2027)

Replace Brooks's immediate public-dashboard task with convening or supporting a community advisory process, developing governance and interpretation criteria, and drafting only citywide descriptive communications for the pilot. (Direction Review — March 18, 2027)

Revise the Chen-Brooks escalation protocol so it governs internal review of subcatchment signals; do not tie it to automatic localized public advisories until governance criteria are established. (Direction Review — March 18, 2027)
tasks_unchanged: Continue collecting aggregated citywide clinical comparison data, although its role is now contextual validation rather than proof of lead time. (Existing Research Plan; Direction Review — March 18, 2027)

Continue assessing flow, rainfall, normalization, laboratory performance, and detection limits as necessary parts of interpreting wastewater trends. (Existing Research Plan; Direction Review — March 18, 2027)

Retain the six-month pilot planning and the need for a sampling, laboratory, and data-transfer budget, revised for the new sites and sampling schedule. (Existing Research Plan; Direction Review — March 18, 2027)

speakers.name: Dr. Maya Chen
speakers.background: Dr. Chen is an infectious-disease epidemiologist with 11 years of experience in municipal surveillance design, including respiratory-virus dashboards, syndromic surveillance, and evaluation of leading indicators against emergency-department and laboratory trends. At Riverton Public Health, she translates surveillance questions into measurable decision rules and works primarily with aggregated, privacy-protected data. She has led evaluations using time-series comparisons, lag analyses, and sensitivity checks rather than treating any single signal as definitive evidence.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Chen frames wastewater surveillance as a decision-support system, not a direct count of infections. She will push the group to specify what public-health action a changing signal could credibly support, what uncertainty must accompany it, and how clinical data can provide context without being used as a simplistic gold standard. She is prepared to revise the original lead-time ambition when operational conditions make it untestable or when localized results cannot be interpreted safely.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

speakers.name: Dr. Hannah Brooks
speakers.background: Dr. Brooks is a postdoctoral researcher in science and technology studies with 5 years of qualitative research experience on public-health data systems, environmental monitoring, and institutional trust. Her methods include semi-structured interviews, facilitated community workshops, document analysis, and observation of cross-agency planning processes. She has worked with neighborhood coalitions to examine how aggregate indicators can acquire social meaning when they are mapped, ranked, or attached to place names.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Brooks treats data governance and communication as part of the surveillance system itself, rather than as an outreach step after technical work is complete. She will emphasize that a subcatchment is not merely a neutral analytic unit: releasing site-specific values can invite inferences about residents, businesses, or neighborhood behavior that the data cannot support. Her central question is what institutional safeguards, community participation, interpretive criteria, and release rules are needed before localized findings can be used or made public.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

speakers.name: Luis Ortega
speakers.background: Luis Ortega is an environmental engineer with 14 years of experience in municipal collection systems, influent monitoring, wet-weather operations, and utility–public-health coordination. As Water Services' project manager, he has overseen field crews, access permitting, sampling equipment deployment, chain-of-custody procedures, and flow-data quality reviews. His work has focused on how sewer hydraulics, industrial inputs, infiltration and inflow, and changing service populations affect what a sample can reasonably represent.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Ortega begins with the physical system: what enters a sampling point, how stable that contributing area is, and whether the utility can collect comparable samples safely and reliably. He will challenge interpretations that exceed the hydraulic reality of the network, especially where stormwater intrusion and broad mixed catchments distort plant-level trends. He sees defined trunk-sewer sites and feasible repeatable sampling as a stronger foundation for a pilot, while remaining cautious about whether engineering measures alone can make a biological signal actionable.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: uncertain about how their methods apply to this problem

meetings.meeting_context:
Riverton Public Health Department is partnering with Riverton University and the municipal Water Services Department to design a pilot wastewater-monitoring program for a city of roughly 280,000 residents. The team has completed an initial plan centered on citywide early warning and public reporting, but is revisiting that plan after receiving new operational and community information.

Direction Review — March 18, 2027. The Riverton wastewater surveillance planning team is meeting to revise the proposed pilot after Water Services reports operational constraints and community partners raise concerns about how localized results could be used. The group needs to decide what the pilot should learn first and which elements of the existing plan should be revised before launch.

The team's current research plan, which everyone has read:
Riverton Wastewater Surveillance Planning Team — Existing Research Plan

Aim: Design a six-month pilot that determines whether wastewater measurements can provide useful early warning of selected infectious diseases in Riverton and establishes a credible approach for sharing the resulting information.

1. Research question 1: Can weekly wastewater measurements at Riverton's two treatment plants detect changes in SARS-CoV-2, influenza A, and norovirus before corresponding changes appear in citywide clinical reporting?

2. Research question 2: Which normalization and laboratory procedures produce sufficiently stable, interpretable trends across the two treatment-plant catchments, given variation in flow, rainfall, and population served?

3. Research question 3: What public-facing reporting format allows residents and decision-makers to understand citywide wastewater trends and their uncertainty, while maintaining trust in the program?

The pilot will compare wastewater signals with aggregated citywide emergency-department and laboratory reports, not individual-level records. The initial geographic unit is the two treatment-plant catchments: North Plant and South Plant. Results will be treated as trend indicators rather than estimates of disease prevalence.

Tasks
1. Dr. Maya Chen (epidemiology) will define lead-time metrics, obtain weekly aggregated clinical comparison data, and specify interpretation thresholds for SARS-CoV-2, influenza A, and norovirus.
2. Luis Ortega (environmental engineering) will document the North and South catchments, select influent sampling points at both plants, assess flow and rainfall effects, and develop a 24-hour composite-sampling protocol.
3. Priya Nair (environmental engineering) will validate RT-qPCR assays and compare normalization using pepper mild mottle virus and measured flow.
4. Dr. Hannah Brooks (science and technology studies) will interview public-health staff, water-utility staff, and residents about confidence in citywide reporting, then draft a public dashboard and uncertainty language.
5. Chen and Brooks will develop an escalation protocol linking sustained wastewater increases to internal public-health review and a public advisory when warranted.
6. Ortega will prepare a sampling, laboratory, and data-transfer budget for the six-month pilot.

seed_spec.benchmark_task:
Part 1 of 1 of a multi-part sample for this benchmark task: Provide an existing research plan and a new meeting that changes the research direction. The evaluated AI must identify old and new questions, explain changes, update relevant tasks and preserve the earlier direction.
Judge this transcript only on its own part: Maya Chen opens by noting that the original plan sought citywide early warning for three pathogens using the two treatment plants and comparison with aggregated clinical data. Luis Ortega reports that both treatment-plant influent streams combine large, heterogeneous areas and that stormwater intrusion at North Plant makes pathogen trends difficult to interpret at the plant level. He states that Water Services can support sampling at three stable trunk-sewer access points serving defined, mostly sanitary subcatchments, but cannot guarantee continuous 24-hour composite sampling at both plants during the pilot; twice-weekly time-weighted composites at the three trunk sites are feasible. Priya Nair states that preliminary method work indicates the assays are reliable for SARS-CoV-2 and influenza A, but norovirus recovery is too variable to support pilot interpretation without a separate method-development effort.

Hannah Brooks reports that neighborhood coalition representatives do not reject wastewater monitoring, but oppose a public dashboard displaying neighborhood-level pathogen values because such displays could stigmatize areas and invite unsupported claims about residents. They support a governance process in which a community advisory group helps determine interpretation and communications before any localized findings are released. The group decides to redirect the pilot toward understanding whether subcatchment signals are technically interpretable and operationally useful for internal, nonpublic public-health response. They retain citywide clinical comparison, but reframe it as contextual validation rather than a promise to demonstrate lead time. They agree that public reporting will be designed only after governance and interpretation criteria are established, and that any initial public communication will be citywide and descriptive rather than site-specific.

The team explicitly replaces the three-pathogen scope with SARS-CoV-2 and influenza A. They leave open whether localized data will ever be publicly released and do not settle final thresholds for operational action. The meeting identifies which plan tasks must be revised, paused, or retained; it does not resolve detailed budgets or final laboratory turnaround times.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Morning—it’s doing that March thing again here, sunny and somehow still freezing. Um, I know we’re all squeezed for time, so I wanted to use this to decide what the pilot can actually learn with the revised field setup. Whether the signals are interpretable enough for internal public-health review, rather than promising a clean lead-time result or a dashboard right away.

transcript.speaker: Luis Ortega
transcript.text: It’s cold at the plants too, which the crews are enjoying. I’m glad we’re narrowing it. The two plant influents can’t- I don’t think they can carry that promise, especially North in rain. We can do twice-weekly time-weighted composites at three trunk sites with much more defined contributing areas, but I need Maya’s sense of what a repeated increase would actually trigger internally, not prove, just trigger.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Hannah Brooks
transcript.text: Hm, defined areas matters.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: A repeated increase could trigger an internal review. We'd look at it alongside the aggregated ED and lab trends and ask if there's anything operational we should be watching. But Luis, I need to know whether those trunk-site populations and drainage boundaries hold steady week to week. If they shift around, I can't write a meaningful review rule yet.

transcript.speaker: Luis Ortega
transcript.text: Mostly, yes. The mapped drainage areas should be stable, and these aren’t sites where we expect regular diversions. But I want to verify that in the field. One candidate had a much bigger flow jump than expected in the first moderate rain. Until we rule out an upstream inflow source or cross-connection, I’d treat wet-weather samples there as potentially not comparable.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Then I’d keep wet-weather samples out of any repeated-increase rule until you’ve checked that site. If there’s a dry-weather rise across the two collections, we could still pull the aggregated ED and lab context. But I don’t want us to treat a rain-driven change like an epidemiologic signal.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Hannah Brooks
transcript.text: That uncertainty is part of the governance question for me. If a site has a rain-related jump or a boundary we’re still verifying, I don’t think it should be visible outside the internal review at all. People will read a mapped line as a statement about that area. Luis, besides rain, are there construction, industrial discharges, or routing changes that could alter who’s effectively contributing to a trunk site?

transcript.speaker: Luis Ortega
transcript.text: Construction is the main thing I'd watch. I don't know of any active routing changes at the three locations. Industrial inputs should be limited at the proposed trunks, but I need to verify the upstream users. And that unexpected rain response is exactly why I'm not ready to call one boundary stable yet. If Hannah's saying no external map while that's still open, that seems sensible.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Mm, that’s a concern.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Hannah Brooks
transcript.text: Even once the engineering checks are done, I’d want a rule that a local signal isn’t treated as a claim about infection in that service area. Maya, if the citywide clinical trend and one trunk signal don’t- if they don’t line up, how would you want staff to talk about that internally without treating one as the obvious “wrong” source?

transcript.speaker: Luis Ortega
transcript.text: Yeah, that’s tricky.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: I’d say they’re answering different questions, not competing measures. A trunk signal is a change in what’s reaching that sewer at that point, and ED and labs reflect care-seeking and testing, with their own delays. Last winter, the ED timing moved just from backlog cleanup. So internally, I’d write, “signal increased, clinical context is rising, flat, or not yet informative,” and then review possible explanations rather than say either one is wrong...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Hannah Brooks
transcript.text: That framing helps, actually. It gives us language for the internal record that doesn't turn a mismatch into a failure or, worse, into a claim about the people upstream. I'd want the advisory group to see it and help shape it before we decide whether any local results are releasable.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Yeah, I'd like that.

transcript.speaker: Luis Ortega
transcript.text: Before that group sees anything, I need to finish the boring physical checks. Access windows, power for the samplers, upstream users, and that rain response at the one site. If the advisory group ends up saying sewer boundaries still- if they still read as neighborhood labels, then even a technically stable trunk result may need to stay internal for this pilot.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: For the pilot, I think that means the public dashboard task pauses, but the internal review record and the citywide clinical feed stay in scope. I still need to check whether those weekly ED and lab extracts arrive consistently enough to be useful context. If they're backfilled unpredictably, then we should- we should label that, rather than pretending we can assess lead time.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Hannah Brooks
transcript.text: I’d pause the dashboard task as it is now, not public-facing work altogether. I can redirect the interviews and workshops toward what an advisory group would need to decide, like who participates, what counts as interpretable enough, and what stays internal. I still need to ask the coalition whether they’d rather nominate people or have an open process.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Okay, let’s see what they prefer.

transcript.speaker: Luis Ortega
transcript.text: One thing I need from that advisory process is whether they see any use in us later publishing just a citywide combined trend, with no trunk-site results at all. The trunks would still be for our operational learning, but I don't want to build a reporting path around them if people are going to read that geography as neighborhood ranking.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: A later citywide combined trend is worth putting to them, but that needs to be separate from the question of releasing trunk results. For me, it would need very plain limits. This is a broad trend, not a map of where illness is. And we shouldn't promise it now while we're still learning whether the clinical context- whether it arrives on time.

transcript.speaker: Luis Ortega
transcript.text: And physically, I’d be careful calling it “citywide” if we’re combining three trunks— three trunk sites won’t represent all of Riverton the same way the plants do. Maybe the advisory group can react to that distinction, but I think we need to be very explicit about what population a combined signal does and doesn’t cover.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Exactly. If those three trunks don't have known, stable coverage of the whole city, I wouldn't combine them into something we call citywide. Maybe later we can report a pilot-level trend for the sampled system, but even that needs the denominator, or really, a clear statement of who isn't represented. Luis, do you have a rough sense of whether the three together miss a large part of Riverton?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Hannah Brooks
transcript.text: Right, that distinction is important.

transcript.speaker: Luis Ortega
transcript.text: Roughly, yes, they miss a substantial share. I’d rather not put a number on it until I rerun the service-area estimates, because the three areas aren’t comparable sizes and that candidate site’s boundary is still, still under question. They’re good places to learn whether repeatable sampling and interpretation are possible, but they’re not a surrogate for Riverton as a whole.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Hannah Brooks
transcript.text: Mm, then I don't think we should even float a public combined trend as "citywide" in the pilot. The people I spoke with were already much more wary once they saw a boundary on a map, and a partial-system trend with unclear coverage could be just as misleading, even without the map. I'd bring that exact distinction to the advisory conversations and see whether there's any, any public use they regard as meaningful.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: I’d make the pilot’s public commitment about governance and learning, not about publishing a trend. Trunk results stay internal, and we use the advisory process to decide what, if anything, could responsibly leave that setting later. I’ll check the extract timing with the clinical-data teams this week because that determines how much comparison we can honestly build into the review record.

transcript.speaker: Luis Ortega
transcript.text: That works for me. I’ll treat the three trunks as an internal feasibility set, not coverage for Riverton, and I’ll come back once I’ve checked access, power, upstream inputs, and that storm response—rain response—before we lock the sites.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Good. Until those checks are back, I’ll revise my piece so it’s not about lead-time metrics. I’ll make it an internal review template with repeat signal, wet-weather status, site notes, and whatever clinical context is available that week. Once we’ve seen a few weeks of actual operations, we can decide whether any threshold is defensible.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Hannah Brooks
transcript.text: That gives the advisory work something real to respond to, rather than a finished dashboard. I’ll check with the coalition on nomination versus open recruitment, and we should make clear from the start that the group is setting release conditions. Not just commenting on wording after the fact.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Okay, I think we can stop there. The rest can wait until next time. Thanks, both. I’ll see you at the next check-in, and then we can—

transcript.speaker: Luis Ortega
transcript.text: All right, take care, both.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Hannah Brooks
transcript.text: Bye, both—stay warm.
